messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Shouting: Shouting, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Fatima is a 38-year-old married woman of Jordanian descent who works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in the outer suburbs of Phoenix. She presented for psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 61, following an assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago and from which she describes herself as never having fully recovered.

On a Tuesday afternoon shift, Fatima was cleaning a room on the fourth floor when a male guest entered the room behind her and locked the door. What followed was a prolonged physical assault during which he restrained her arms and forced her to remain in the room despite her attempts to leave. She recalls with terrible precision the sound of his voice rising — the way his shouting filled the small space and seemed to leave no air for her — and the sensation of her wrists being held against her will, her body made to stay where she did not choose to stay. Other parts of that hour are gone entirely. She cannot account for stretches of time that she knows passed, and the gaps themselves disturb her, as though the missing pieces contain something she is not yet able to hold. She has described the memory as a series of photographs with whole pages torn out between them, and she has come to feel that she is only ever working with a partial account of what happened to her — that the full truth of it exists somewhere she cannot access.

In the months that followed, Fatima returned to work twice before stopping altogether. The hotel corridors, the sound of a room door closing behind her, the sight of a housekeeping cart — each of these had become intolerable. More specifically, any moment in which someone else's instruction or presence constrained what she could do with her body would produce an immediate and overwhelming response. Her supervisor, a well-meaning woman, once asked her firmly to finish a room before her break, and Fatima had to leave the building. She understood, on some level, that this was a reasonable workplace request. What she could not explain, even to herself, was that being required to stay somewhere she had not chosen to stay no longer felt like a scheduling matter. She has not returned to hotel work since, and the loss of income has placed significant strain on her marriage, with her husband taking on additional shifts and the two of them speaking less than they once did.

At home, Fatima moves through her days in a state of sustained alertness. She listens for the sound of the front door, for footsteps in the hallway, for any indication that someone might be entering the house without her full awareness. She positions herself in rooms so that she can see the entrance. When a neighbor's television carries raised voices through the shared wall, she goes rigid. Shouting — even the muffled, ordinary kind — lands in her body before her mind can contextualize it. On several occasions the memory has returned with a physical dimension she had not anticipated: a tightening across her wrists, a pressure in her shoulders, sensations she recognizes as belonging to that afternoon even when nothing in her present environment has changed. Concentration has become difficult in a way that compounds her distress; she begins tasks and loses them, reads a sentence and finds it gone.

She has avoided the news stories covering a subsequent assault at the same hotel chain. She cannot say exactly what she fears she will feel if she sees coverage of another victim, only that the thought of it produces something close to dread.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was her youngest daughter's school play last spring, at which another parent raised their voice during a parking dispute outside the auditorium. Fatima spent the performance in the lobby, unable to go back inside. She told her husband afterward that she did not recognize herself anymore. She arrived at her first session hoping, above all, to feel safe in her own home — and afraid, most deeply, that the parts of the memory she cannot reach are the parts that would finally explain why she is not.
